The Levites ask for their appointed cities (verses 1–8)

The Levites waited until the other tribes had received their portions before bringing their request to Joshua.

They based the request not on their own excellence or service but on God's command.

Support for ministers is not something a congregation may leave entirely to personal whim, as though it were free to let its ministers starve.

Those who preach the gospel should live from the gospel and should be able to live adequately.

The Levites live among the tribes (verses 9–42)

The Levites were distributed among Israel's other tribes.

They knew that the whole nation was watching them.

They therefore needed to live carefully so that no one could justly criticize their ministry.

Every tribe received some cities for the Levites.

This was God's gracious way of preserving true religion and making knowledge of his word available throughout the land.

Blessed be God that, under the gospel, his word has been spread more widely among us.

The Lord fulfills his promises (<reference osisRef="Josh.21.43-Josh.21.45" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 43–45</reference>)

God had promised Abraham's descendants the land of Canaan.

Now they occupied it and settled there.

The promise of the heavenly Canaan is just as certain for all God's spiritual Israel, because it comes from the One who cannot lie.

No enemy could stand against them.

The Canaanites' later successes resulted from Israel's failure to act diligently and from its sinful willingness to tolerate the surrounding people's idolatry and wickedness.

Not one good thing God had promised Israel failed to come true.

At the proper time, all his promises will be fulfilled.

Then his people will acknowledge that the Lord has exceeded their greatest hopes, made them more than conquerors and brought them into the rest they desired.

Verses 1-8
The Levites waited till the other tribes were provided for, before they preferred their claim to Joshua. They build their claim upon a very good foundation; not their own merits or services, but the Divine precept. The maintenance of ministers is not a thing left merely to the will of the people, that they may let them starve if they please; they which preach the gospel should live by the gospel, and should live comfortably. ( [Josh.21.9-Josh.21.42] Jos 21:9-42)
[Josh.21.9-Josh.21.42]
Verses 9-42
By mixing the Levites with the other tribes, they were made to see that the eyes of all Israel were upon them, and therefore it was their concern to walk so that their ministry might not be blamed. Every tribe had its share of Levites' cities. Thus did God graciously provide for keeping up religion among them, and that they might have the word in all parts of the land. Yet, blessed be God, we have the gospel more diffused amongst us. ( [Josh.21.43-Josh.21.45] Jos 21:43-45)
[Josh.21.43-Josh.21.45]
Verses 43-45
God promised to give to the seed of Abraham the land of Canaan for a possession, and now they possessed it, and dwelt therein. And the promise of the heavenly Canaan is as sure to all God's spiritual Israel; for it is the promise of Him that cannot lie. There stood not a man before them. The after-prevalence of the Canaanites was the effect of Israel's slothfulness, and the punishment of their sinful inclination to the idolatries and abominations of the heathen whom they harboured and indulged. There failed not aught of any good thing, which the Lord had spoken to the house of Israel. In due season all his promises will be accomplished; then will his people acknowledge that the Lord has exceeded their largest expectations, and made them more than conquerors, and brought them to their desired rest.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesReuben and Gad, with the half tribe of Manasseh, dismissed to their homes.1–9They build an altar of testimony, The congregation offended thereat.10–20The answer of the Reubenites.21–29The children of Israel satisfied.30–34
The eastern tribes return home (verses 1–9)

Joshua dismissed these tribes with sound counsel.

Receiving a command is useless unless we obey it. We cannot obey rightly without paying careful attention.

Above all, we must love the Lord our God as the best of all beings and the best of friends.

As far as love governs the heart, we will continually seek to follow his ways, even when those ways are narrow and difficult, and to keep every one of his commands.

In every circumstance, we must purpose from the heart to cling to the Lord and serve him and his kingdom among people, with all our heart and soul.

This good counsel applies to everyone. May God give us grace to accept it!

The eastern tribes build an altar and cause concern (verses 10–20)

The tribes living east of the Jordan wanted to remain connected to Israel's worship.

At first their new altar seemed like an attempt to establish a rival to the altar at Shiloh.

God is jealous for the worship he has appointed, and we should be concerned about anything that resembles or leads to idolatry.

Corruption in religion is best confronted at its beginning.

But the Israelites' prudence in investigating their concern was no less commendable than their zeal to protect worship.

Many bitter disputes could be prevented or quickly resolved if people would first inquire into the alleged offense.

Remembering great sins committed earlier should make us watchful against sin's beginnings: the path of sin slopes downward.

We must warn a neighbor who does wrong, rather than allow that person to continue uncorrected (Leviticus 19:17).

The western tribes even offered to welcome their brothers to settle in the land where the Lord's tabernacle stood.

That generous offer expressed the true spirit of Israel.

The eastern tribes explain the altar (verses 21–29)

The eastern tribes received their brothers' criticism patiently.

They gave their explanation with humility and solemnity, doing everything possible to satisfy the others.

They spoke God's name with reverence.

Their brief confession of faith removed the suspicion that they intended to worship other gods.

We should always speak of God seriously and pause with reverence when mentioning his name.

A careless expression such as “God knows” may misuse his name.

But God truly does know everything, including our deepest thoughts and intentions.

In every religious act, it matters above all that we are sincere before him.

Yet we should also let other people recognize that sincerity by its fruits, especially when those who misunderstand us are genuinely concerned for God's glory.

The tribes rejected the evil purpose they were accused of and clearly explained the altar's true intention.

People who have received the benefits of God's appointed worship naturally want to preserve those blessings for their children.

They should take every appropriate step to ensure that their descendants are recognized as part of God's people.

Christ is the great Altar who makes every gift acceptable.

The clearest evidence that we belong to him is the work of his Spirit in our hearts.

Israel accepts the explanation and peace is restored (verses 30–34)

It was good that both sides wanted peace as well as faithfulness to God.

Religious disagreements can become especially fierce and difficult to resolve when wisdom and love are lacking.

Proud, irritable people may refuse to withdraw an accusation even when clear evidence shows they were wrong.

Israel did not act in that spirit.

The western tribes recognized their brothers' innocence as a sign of God's presence.

We should be glad when fears about another Christian's faithfulness prove unfounded and we discover that the person genuinely loves God and seeks holiness.

The altar was named Ed, meaning witness.

It testified to the tribes' determination to preserve pure worship, and it would stand as a warning to their descendants if they later abandoned the Lord.

How happy it would be if all professing Christians learned from Israel's example!

We need zeal and steadiness for God's truth together with fairness, gentleness, willingness to understand, readiness to explain and readiness to accept a brother's explanation.

May the Lord increase the number who preserve the Spirit's unity through the bond of peace.

May grace and comfort increase among everyone who sincerely loves Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Josh.22.1-Josh.22.9]
Chapter 22
Chapter Outline
Reuben and Gad, with the half tribe of Manasseh, dismissed to their homes. | (1-9) |
They build an altar of testimony, The congregation offended thereat. | (10-20) |
The answer of the Reubenites. | (21-29) |
The children of Israel satisfied. | (30-34) |
Verses 1-9
Joshua dismisses the tribes with good counsel. Those who have the commandment have it in vain, unless they do the commandment; and it will not be done aright unless we take diligent heed. In particular to love the Lord our God, as the best of beings, and the best of friends; and as far as that principle rules in the heart, there will be constant care and endeavour to walk in his ways, even those that are narrow and up-hill. In every instance to keep his commandments. At all times, and in all conditions, with purpose of heart to cleave unto the Lord, and to serve him and his kingdom among men, with all our heart, and with all our soul. This good counsel is given to all; may God give us grace to take it!
[Josh.22.10-Josh.22.20]
Verses 10-20
Here is the care of the separated tribes to keep their hold of Canaan's religion. At first sight it seemed a design to set up an altar against the altar at Shiloh. God is jealous for his own institutions; we should be so too, and afraid of every thing that looks like, or leads to idolatry. Corruptions in religion are best dealt with at first. But their prudence in following up this zealous resolution is no less commendable. Many an unhappy strife would be prevented, or soon made up, by inquiries into the matter of the offence. The remembrance of great sins committed formerly, should engage us to stand on our guard against the beginnings of sin; for the way of sin is down-hill. We are all concerned to reprove our neighbour when he does amiss, lest we suffer sin upon him, [Lev.19.17] Le 19:17. The offer made that they should be welcome to come to the land where the Lord's tabernacle was, and settle there, was in the spirit of true Israelites.
[Josh.22.21-Josh.22.29]
Verses 21-29
The tribes took the reproofs of their brethren in good part. With solemnity and meekness they proceeded to give all the satisfaction in their power. Reverence of God is expressed in the form of their appeal. This brief confession of faith would remove their brethren's suspicion that they intended to worship other gods. Let us always speak of God with seriousness, and mention his name with a solemn pause. Those who make appeals to Heaven with a careless "God knows," take his name in vain: it is very unlike this. They express great confidence of their own uprightness in the matter of their appeal. "God knows it," for he is perfectly acquainted with the thoughts and intents of the heart. In every thing we do in religion, it highly concerns us to approve ourselves to God, remembering that he knows the heart. And if our sincerity be known to God, we should study likewise to let others know it by its fruits, especially those who, though they mistake us, show zeal for the glory of God. They disdained the design of which they were suspected to be guilty, and fully explained their true intent in building this altar. Those who have found the comfort and benefit of God's ordinances, cannot but desire to preserve them to their seed, and to use all possible care that their children may be looked upon as having a part in him. Christ is the great Altar that sanctifies every gift; the best evidence of our interest in him is the work of his Spirit in our hearts.
[Josh.22.30-Josh.22.34]
Verses 30-34
It is well that there was on both sides a disposition to peace, as there was a zeal for God; for quarrels about religion, for want of wisdom and love, often prove the most fierce and difficult to be made up. Proud and peevish spirits, when they have passed any unjust blame on their brethren, though full evidence be brought of its unfairness, can by no means be persuaded to withdraw it. But Israel was not so prejudiced. They looked upon their brethren's innocence as a token of God's presence. Our brethren's zeal for the power of godliness, and faith and love, notwithstanding the fears of their breaking the unity of the church, are things of which we should be very glad to be satisfied. The altar was called ED, a witness. It was a witness of their care to keep their religion pure and entire, and would witness against their descendants, if they should turn from following after the Lord. Happy will it be when all professed Christians learn to copy the example of Israel, to unite zeal and steady adherence to the cause of truth, with candour, meekness, and readiness to understand each other, to explain and to be satisfied with the explanations of their brethren. May the Lord increase the number of those who endeavour to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace! may increasing grace and consolation be with all who love Jesus Christ in sincerity!

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJoshua's exhortation before his death.1–10Joshua warns the people of idolatry.11–16
Joshua urges faithfulness before his death (verses 1–10)

Joshua was old and near death. The people therefore had special reason to listen carefully to his words.

He reminded them of the great things God had done during his leadership.

He urged them to be very courageous.

They must take care to keep what Scripture says, diligently do it and sincerely respect it.

They must also work cautiously to remove every reminder of pagan idolatry, so that its worship would never return.

Henry laments how casually people who call themselves Christians use the names of pagan gods, making them familiar in everyday conversation.

Joshua called Israel to perseverance.

There may have been many faults among the people, but they had not altogether abandoned the Lord their God.

One way to help people become better is first to recognize whatever good is already present in them.

Joshua warns Israel against idolatry (verses 11–16)

If we want to remain close to the Lord, we must stay watchful. Many souls are lost through sheer carelessness.

Love God, and you will not want to leave him.

He has remained faithful to you; do not be unfaithful to him.

The One who promised is faithful (Hebrews 10:23).

Every Christian's experience confirms this truth.

Struggles may be long and difficult, and trials may be numerous and severe.

Yet in the end the believer will acknowledge that goodness and mercy followed throughout life.

Joshua explained exactly how apostasy would progress.

First, the people would become friends with idolaters.

Next, they would intermarry with them.

Finally, they would worship their gods.

Sin's path runs downhill. People who deliberately share fellowship with sinners cannot avoid becoming involved in sin.

Joshua warned that such a course would destroy them.

The excellence of the heavenly Canaan, and God's freely given and unfailing promise of it, will only deepen the misery of people who remain excluded from it forever.

Their awareness of how happy they might have been will make them see more clearly how miserable they have become.

Let us watch and pray against temptation.

Let us trust God's faithfulness, love and power, appeal to his promises and cling to his commands.

Then we will be blessed in life, in death and forever.
classic_reading:
[Josh.23.1-Josh.23.10]
Chapter 23
Chapter Outline
Joshua's exhortation before his death. | (1-10) |
Joshua warns the people of idolatry. | (11-16) |
Verses 1-10
Joshua was old and dying, let them observe what he said now. He put them in mind of the great things God had done for them in his days. He exhorted them to be very courageous. Keep with care, do with diligence, and regard with sincerity what is written. Also, very cautiously to endeavour that the heathen idolatry may be forgotten, so that it may never be revived. It is sad that among Christians the names of the heathen gods are so commonly used, and made so familiar as they are. Joshua exhorts them to be very constant. There might be many things amiss among them, but they had not forsaken the Lord their God; the way to make people better, is to make the best of them.
[Josh.23.11-Josh.23.16]
Verses 11-16
Would we cleave to the Lord, we must always stand upon our guard, for many a soul is lost through carelessness. Love the Lord your God, and you will not leave him. Has God been thus true to you? Be not you false to him. He is faithful that has promised, [Heb.10.23] He 10:23. The experience of every Christian witnesses the same truth. Conflicts may have been severe and long, trials great and many; but at the last he will acknowledge that goodness and mercy followed him all the days of his life. Joshua states the fatal consequences of going back; know for a certainty it will be your ruin. The first step would be, friendship with idolaters; the next would be, marrying with them; the end of that would be, serving their gods. Thus the way of sin is down-hill, and those who have fellowship with sinners, cannot avoid having fellowship with sin. He describes the destruction he warns them of. The goodness of the heavenly Canaan, and the free and sure grant God has made of it, will add to the misery of those who shall for ever be shut out from it. Nothing will make them see how wretched they are, so much, as to see how happy they might have been. Let us watch and pray against temptation. Let us trust in God's faithfulness, love, and power; let us plead his promises, and cleave to his commandments, then we shall be happy in life, in death, and for ever.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod's benefits to their fathers.1–14Joshua renews the covenant between the people and God.15–28Joshua's death, Joseph's bones buried, The state of Israel.29–33
Joshua recalls God's goodness (verses 1–14)

We should never consider our work for God finished until our lives are finished.

If God gives us more years than we expected, as he gave Joshua, it is because we still have work to do.

Anyone seeking to have the mind of Jesus Christ should be glad to give a final testimony to the Savior's goodness.

We should tell everyone around us how deeply God's undeserved kindness obligates us to him.

Israel gathered in solemn worship.

Joshua addressed the people in God's name and as his messenger.

His address had two parts: teaching and application.

In the first, Joshua recalled the great things God had done for Israel and for the generations before them.

Then he applied that history of mercy by urging the people to fear and serve the Lord out of gratitude, so that his favor might continue among them.

Joshua calls Israel to choose and renew the covenant (verses 15–28)

God's people must serve him with willing minds.

Love is the only genuine principle from which acceptable service to God can spring.

The Father seeks worshipers who worship in spirit and truth.

Our natural, fleshly minds are hostile to God and cannot perform such spiritual worship.

We therefore must be born again.

Many people are content with outward religious forms, which they regard as imposed duties rather than a delight.

Joshua told the people to choose whom they would serve.

He did not mean that serving God was an optional matter of indifference.

He set the issue clearly before them and declared his own decision, whatever others might do.

Those traveling toward heaven must be willing to go against the current.

They must not simply follow the majority, but follow the example of the best.

No one can live faithfully in any position without serious attention to religious duties in family life.

Israel responded, “We also will serve the Lord.”

Joshua's example had a powerful influence because he had been such a blessing to the people.

People with great influence can do much good when they are zealous for true faith.

Joshua led them to express a sincere determination to cling to God.

But they needed to abandon every confidence in their own strength.

Without God's help, their resolutions would fail.

After they had deliberately chosen to serve God, Joshua bound them to that decision through a solemn covenant.

He erected a memorial.

In this moving way, he took his final leave of them.

If they later perished through rebellion, they would bear responsibility for their own blood.

The house of God, the Lord's table and even the walls and trees before which we have made solemn promises could testify against us if we turn away from him.

Yet we may trust God to put his reverence within our hearts so that we will not abandon him.

Only God can grant saving grace.

Nevertheless, he blesses our efforts to encourage others to serve him.

Joshua dies; Joseph's bones are buried (verses 29–33)

Joseph died in Egypt but commanded that his bones should not finally remain there.

He wanted them brought to the promised land once Israel had entered its rest.

Joshua also died and was buried, as was Eleazar the high priest.

Even the most useful servants of God eventually die, having served their generation according to his will.

One after another, they fall asleep and their bodies decay.

But Jesus, who completed his earthly life with a saving work far greater than that of Joshua or Joseph, rose from the dead and did not undergo corruption.

Those whom the Lord has redeemed will inherit the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

In amazement at Jesus' grace, they will declare:

To him who loved us and washed us from our sins by his own blood, and made us kings and priests to God his Father—to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
classic_reading:
[Josh.24.1-Josh.24.14]
Chapter 24
Chapter Outline
God's benefits to their fathers. | (1-14) |
Joshua renews the covenant between the people and God. | (15-28) |
Joshua's death, Joseph's bones buried, The state of Israel. | (29-33) |
Verses 1-14
We must never think our work for God done, till our life is done. If he lengthen out our days beyond what we expected, like those of Joshua, it is because he has some further service for us to do. He who aims at the same mind which was in Christ Jesus, will glory in bearing the last testimony to his Saviour's goodness, and in telling to all around, the obligations with which the unmerited goodness of God has bound him. The assembly came together in a solemn religious manner. Joshua spake to them in God's name, and as from him. His sermon consists of doctrine and application. The doctrinal part is a history of the great things God had done for his people, and for their fathers before them. The application of this history of God's mercies to them, is an exhortation to fear and serve God, in gratitude for his favour, and that it might be continued.
[Josh.24.15-Josh.24.28]
Verses 15-28
It is essential that the service of God's people be performed with a willing mind. For LOVE is the only genuine principle whence all acceptable service of God can spring. The Father seeks only such to worship him, as worship him in spirit and in truth. The carnal mind of man is enmity against God, therefore, is not capable of such spiritual worship. Hence the necessity of being born again. But numbers rest in mere forms, as tasks imposed upon them. Joshua puts them to their choice; but not as if it were indifferent whether they served God or not. Choose you whom ye will serve, now the matter is laid plainly before you. He resolves to do this, whatever others did. Those that are bound for heaven, must be willing to swim against the stream. They must not do as the most do, but as the best do. And no one can behave himself as he ought in any station, who does not deeply consider his religious duties in family relations. The Israelites agree with Joshua, being influenced by the example of a man who had been so great a blessing to them; We also will serve the Lord. See how much good great men do, by their influence, if zealous in religion. Joshua brings them to express full purpose of heart to cleave to the Lord. They must come off from all confidence in their own sufficiency, else their purposes would be in vain. The service of God being made their deliberate choice, Joshua binds them to it by a solemn covenant. He set up a monument of it. In this affecting manner Joshua took his last leave of them; if they perished, their blood would be upon their own heads. Though the house of God, the Lord's table, and even the walls and trees before which we have uttered our solemn purposes of serving him, would bear witness against us if we deny him, yet we may trust in him, that he will put his fear into our hearts, that we shall not depart from him. God alone can give grace, yet he blesses our endeavours to engage men to his service.
[Josh.24.29-Josh.24.33]
Verses 29-33
Joseph died in Egypt, but gave commandment concerning his bones, that they should not rest in their grave till Israel had rest in the land of promise. Notice also the death and burial of Joshua, and of Eleazar the chief priest. The most useful men, having served their generation, according to the will of God, one after another, fall asleep and see corruption. But Jesus, having spent and ended his life on earth more effectually than either Joshua or Joseph, rose from the dead, and saw no corruption. And the redeemed of the Lord shall inherit the kingdom he prepared for them from the foundation of the world. They will say in admiration of the grace of Jesus, Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, and hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father, to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
